questions.stem: What does the term acute coronary syndrome cover?
questions.why: ACS is the spectrum of acute coronary ischemia: unstable angina at one end, NSTEMI in the middle, STEMI at the other. All three share a mechanism — a disrupted plaque with thrombus.

options.t: Stable angina and heart failure of any cause
options.why: Stable angina is a chronic pattern, and heart failure is a separate problem.

options.t: Only ST-elevation myocardial infarction
options.why: STEMI is one member of the group, not the whole of it.

options.t: Any chest pain of cardiac or non-cardiac origin
options.why: The term is specific to coronary ischemia, not to chest pain generally.

options.t: Unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI together

questions.stem: What separates stable angina from unstable angina?
questions.why: Stable angina is predictable — a set amount of exertion brings it on, and rest or nitroglycerin relieves it. When it arrives at rest, lasts longer, or takes less to trigger, the plaque has become unstable.

options.t: Unstable angina shows ST elevation on the 12-lead
options.why: Unstable angina classically has no ST elevation.

options.t: Unstable angina comes at rest or with a changed pattern
Stable angina lasts longer than twenty minutes
options.why: Prolonged pain points away from stable angina, not toward it.

options.t: Stable angina occurs only in patients over sixty
options.why: Age does not define the pattern.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an NSTEMI from unstable angina?
questions.why: Both can look identical in the field — ischemic pain without ST elevation. The difference is troponin: an NSTEMI has damaged enough muscle to release markers, which means it is a diagnosis made at the hospital.

options.t: An NSTEMI shows ST elevation on the 12-lead
options.why: By definition, an NSTEMI has no ST elevation.

options.t: An NSTEMI causes pain lasting under five minutes
options.why: Duration does not distinguish the two.

options.t: Unstable angina involves a completely occluded artery
options.why: Complete occlusion is the STEMI mechanism.

options.t: An NSTEMI has released cardiac markers

questions.stem: Which patient groups most often present with an atypical picture of ACS?
questions.why: Diabetic neuropathy blunts pain, and women and the elderly more often present with dyspnea, fatigue, nausea or weakness instead of crushing chest pain. A high index of suspicion is what catches those infarcts.

options.t: Young men with a strong family history
options.why: That group typically presents with the classic pattern.

options.t: Athletes with a low resting heart rate
options.why: Fitness does not change how ischemic pain is felt.

options.t: Women, diabetics and the elderly
Patients on beta blockers for hypertension
options.why: Beta blockers blunt the tachycardic response but do not usually alter the character of the pain.

questions.stem: Which findings point toward left-sided rather than right-sided heart failure?
questions.why: The failing left ventricle backs fluid into the lungs. The failing right ventricle backs it into the systemic veins — legs, liver, abdomen and neck. Which side failed determines where the fluid goes.

options.t: Ascites with an enlarged spleen
options.why: Abdominal fluid accumulation reflects right-sided congestion.

options.t: Crackles, orthopnea and pink frothy sputum
Cool extremities with a narrowed pulse pressure
options.why: Those signal low output generally, without localizing to a side.

options.t: Peripheral edema, JVD and hepatomegaly
options.why: Those are the classic right-sided findings.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure?
questions.why: When the left ventricle fails, pressure backs into the pulmonary circulation, and the right ventricle eventually fails pushing against it. Right failure from a lung problem alone is cor pulmonale.

options.t: A right coronary artery infarct
options.why: An RV infarct is a real cause but accounts for a small share of cases.

options.t: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.why: COPD does cause cor pulmonale, though it is less common than the left-sided cause.

options.t: A pulmonary embolism
options.why: A large PE can cause acute right failure, but it is not the usual cause.

options.t: Left-sided heart failure

questions.stem: Why does CPAP help a patient in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
questions.why: CPAP forces fluid out of the alveoli and back into the circulation, recruits collapsed alveoli, and raises intrathoracic pressure — which lowers venous return and gives the overloaded left ventricle less to move.

options.t: It delivers a higher oxygen concentration than a mask
options.why: A non-rebreather delivers a comparable concentration; the pressure is what helps.

options.t: It dries the alveolar fluid by increasing airflow
options.why: Air movement does not evaporate alveolar edema.

options.t: Positive pressure pushes fluid back and cuts preload
It reduces the work of the heart by slowing the rate
options.why: CPAP does not act directly on heart rate.

questions.stem: A patient in pulmonary edema is hypotensive at 82 systolic. How does that change your approach?
questions.why: Pulmonary edema with hypotension is cardiogenic shock, not simple congestion. Nitroglycerin needs an adequate pressure to be safe; below that threshold the patient needs pressure support instead.

options.t: A fluid bolus is given to raise the pressure
options.why: Adding volume to a patient already in pulmonary edema worsens the congestion.

options.t: CPAP is contraindicated at any blood pressure this low
options.why: CPAP is used cautiously at low pressures rather than absolutely ruled out.

options.t: Nitroglycerin is withheld and the low pressure is addressed
Nitroglycerin is given at a higher dose to reduce afterload
options.why: Nitroglycerin drops preload and would worsen the hypotension.

questions.stem: What defines cardiogenic shock?
questions.why: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure. The volume and the vessels may be fine; the muscle simply cannot move blood forward, most often after a large anterior infarct.

options.t: The heart cannot pump enough to perfuse the tissues
Circulating volume has dropped below what is needed
options.why: That is hypovolemic shock.

options.t: The vessels have dilated beyond the volume available
options.why: That is distributive shock.

options.t: Something outside the heart is blocking its filling
options.why: That is obstructive shock — tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or a massive PE.

questions.stem: Why can a fluid bolus be harmful in cardiogenic shock?
questions.why: Preload is not the problem — the pump is. Adding volume raises filling pressure behind a ventricle that cannot keep up and pushes more fluid into the lungs.

options.t: Fluid dilutes the cardiac medications already given
options.why: Dilution is not the mechanism of harm here.

options.t: Fluid triggers a reflex bradycardia in these patients
options.why: There is no such reliable reflex.

options.t: The ventricle cannot move the volume it has
Crystalloid cannot cross into the vascular space
options.why: Crystalloid enters the vasculature immediately when infused.

questions.stem: Which chest pain description most suggests aortic dissection?
questions.why: Dissection is abrupt and maximal at onset — patients describe tearing or ripping, often between the shoulder blades. A blood pressure difference between the arms or an unequal pulse supports it.

options.t: Sharp pain that worsens with each deep breath
options.why: Pleuritic pain points toward the lungs or the pericardium.

options.t: Gradual pressure that builds over several hours
options.why: Gradual onset fits an evolving infarct better than a dissection.

options.t: Burning discomfort that eases after eating
options.why: That pattern suggests a gastrointestinal cause.

options.t: Sudden, tearing pain that radiates to the back

questions.stem: Why is aspirin withheld when aortic dissection is strongly suspected?
questions.why: Dissection is a tear in the aortic wall. An antiplatelet drug makes bleeding from that tear worse — which is why a tearing, radiating pain with unequal pulses should give you pause before the aspirin goes in.

options.t: It masks the pain and delays the diagnosis
options.why: Aspirin at this dose is not being given for pain.

options.t: It has no effect on the coronary arteries in dissection
options.why: The reason to withhold it is the bleeding risk, not a lack of effect.

options.t: It interacts with the antihypertensives used in treatment
options.why: There is no such interaction driving this decision.

options.t: It worsens bleeding from an already torn vessel wall

questions.stem: What three findings make up Beck's triad?
questions.why: Beck's triad points at tamponade: distended neck veins from blocked filling, muffled heart tones from fluid around the heart, and a narrowing pulse pressure as stroke volume falls. All three together are uncommon — one or two should still raise the question.

options.t: Hypotension, tachycardia and cool, clammy skin
options.why: Those describe shock in general, without pointing to the pericardium.

options.t: Bradycardia, hypertension and irregular breathing
options.why: That is Cushing's triad, which signals rising intracranial pressure.

options.t: Distended neck veins, muffled tones, narrow pulse pressure
Chest pain, dyspnea and diaphoresis
options.why: Those are common to many cardiac presentations.

questions.stem: Why does even a small volume of blood cause tamponade in an acute injury?
questions.why: A pericardium filling slowly over weeks stretches to hold a litre or more. Filled suddenly, it has not adapted — 100 to 150 mL is enough to stop the heart from filling.

options.t: Blood clots faster inside the pericardial sac
options.why: Clotting speed is not what produces the hemodynamic collapse.

options.t: Acute blood is denser than a chronic effusion
options.why: Density is not a meaningful difference here.

options.t: The heart contracts harder against a fresh effusion
options.why: The heart's response does not explain why volume tolerance is so low.

options.t: The pericardium has no time to stretch

questions.stem: What separates a hypertensive emergency from hypertensive urgency?
questions.why: Both involve severely elevated pressure. It becomes an emergency when an organ is being damaged now — neurologic changes, pulmonary edema, chest pain, visual loss, renal injury.

options.t: Evidence of end-organ damage
Symptoms lasting more than 24 hours
options.why: Duration is not the dividing line.

options.t: A systolic pressure above 180 mmHg
options.why: A number alone does not distinguish the two.

options.t: Failure of the patient's own medication to control it
options.why: Uncontrolled hypertension is common and is not itself an emergency.

questions.stem: Why is pressure lowered gradually rather than quickly in a hypertensive emergency?
questions.why: In chronic hypertension the brain and kidneys shift their autoregulatory range upward. Dropping the pressure to a textbook normal can leave those organs under-perfused at a number that looks fine on the monitor.

options.t: Autoregulation has reset, so a fast drop starves
The medications available cannot act quickly enough
options.why: Several agents act within minutes; the caution is deliberate.

options.t: Slow reduction prevents rebound hypertension later
options.why: Rebound is a concern with abruptly stopping medication, not with controlled lowering.

options.t: A rapid drop triggers reflex bradycardia and arrest
options.why: Reflex tachycardia is the more usual response to a falling pressure.

questions.stem: A young patient has chest pain, fever, and a recent viral illness. Which cardiac diagnosis should you consider?
questions.why: Viral myocarditis can produce chest pain, ST changes, dysrhythmias and heart failure in an otherwise healthy young person. A recent viral illness in a young patient with cardiac complaints should raise it.

options.t: Acute myocardial infarction from plaque rupture
options.why: Possible at any age but far less likely in this picture.

options.t: Aortic dissection
options.why: Dissection presents abruptly and does not follow a viral illness.

options.t: Stable angina
options.why: Stable angina is exertional and does not come with fever.

options.t: Myocarditis

questions.stem: How does pericarditis chest pain typically behave with position?
questions.why: Pericarditis pain is sharp, pleuritic, and worse lying flat — sitting up and leaning forward pulls the inflamed pericardium away from the diaphragm. That positional pattern is a useful discriminator from ischemic pain.

options.t: It is unchanged by any position
options.why: Positional change is one of its more characteristic features.

options.t: It eases lying flat on the back
options.why: Lying flat usually makes pericarditis pain worse.

options.t: It eases only with nitroglycerin
options.why: Nitroglycerin relieves ischemic pain, not inflammatory pericardial pain.

options.t: It eases on sitting up

questions.stem: Why does a patient with severe aortic stenosis tolerate nitroglycerin poorly?
questions.why: With a narrowed outflow tract, stroke volume is fixed. Dropping preload and dilating the periphery lowers pressure with no way for the heart to compensate — the pressure can fall abruptly and not recover.

options.t: Stenosis causes the drug to pool in the left atrium
options.why: Drugs do not pool in a chamber that way.

options.t: A fixed obstruction means output cannot rise
The drug is metabolized abnormally in valve disease
options.why: Metabolism is unchanged by valvular disease.

options.t: Nitroglycerin constricts the stenotic valve further
options.why: Nitroglycerin has no direct effect on valve tissue.

questions.stem: A patient with an LVAD has no palpable pulse and no readable blood pressure but is awake and talking. What does this mean?
questions.why: Continuous-flow LVADs move blood without generating a pulse, so pulse and standard cuff pressures do not apply. Assess mental status, skin and capnography instead — and call the VAD coordinator, whose number the patient carries.

options.t: The blood pressure cuff is faulty and needs replacing
options.why: Standard cuffs frequently cannot read a continuous-flow patient.

options.t: The patient is in profound shock despite appearing well
options.why: Mental status is the better perfusion indicator here, and it is intact.

options.t: The device has failed and the patient is in arrest
options.why: A patient who is awake and talking is perfusing.

options.t: Continuous-flow devices often produce no pulse

questions.stem: A patient reports their implanted defibrillator has shocked them three times in the last hour. What does that indicate?
questions.why: Repeated shocks usually mean recurrent ventricular dysrhythmia — the device is doing its job, and the underlying rhythm is the problem. That patient is monitored, has IV access, and goes to the hospital.

options.t: The device is malfunctioning and should be deactivated
options.why: Repeated appropriate shocks are far more likely than malfunction.

options.t: The patient is imagining the sensation from anxiety
options.why: Patients feel these shocks distinctly, and dismissing the report is unsafe.

options.t: A recurring dysrhythmia the device keeps treating
The battery is failing and discharging at random
options.why: A failing battery stops delivering therapy rather than delivering more.

questions.stem: Which syncope history is most concerning for a cardiac cause?
questions.why: Exertional syncope without warning suggests the heart could not raise output when it was needed — outflow obstruction, a dysrhythmia, or ischemia. Sudden, unheralded and during effort are the features that should worry you.

options.t: Syncope during exertion, with no warning
Syncope after prolonged standing in a warm room
options.why: That is the classic vasovagal setup.

options.t: Syncope preceded by nausea, sweating and tunnel vision
options.why: That prodrome is typical of a vasovagal episode.

options.t: Syncope after standing up quickly from a chair
options.why: That pattern suggests an orthostatic cause.

questions.stem: What does the OPQRST mnemonic organize?
questions.why: Onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity and time structure the story of the complaint. In chest pain, each element is doing diagnostic work — sudden and tearing reads very differently from gradual and pressure-like.

options.t: The components of the primary survey
options.why: The primary survey is organized by the ABCs.

options.t: The reversible causes of pulseless electrical activity
options.why: Those are the Hs and Ts.

options.t: The history of the present complaint
The order of interventions in a cardiac arrest
options.why: Arrest interventions run off the ACLS algorithms.

questions.stem: Match each shock category to its underlying failure.
questions.why: Every shock is a failure of the pump, the volume, or the container — plus obstruction as a fourth. Naming the category tells you whether to give fluid, support pressure, or relieve an obstruction.
pairs: Cardiogenic
The pump cannot move blood forward
Hypovolemic
There is not enough volume in the system
Distributive
The vessels have dilated beyond the volume
Obstructive
Something outside the heart blocks filling or outflow
Neurogenic
Lost sympathetic tone leaves vessels dilated and the rate slow
Anaphylactic
Massive mediator release dilates vessels and leaks fluid

questions.stem: Match each heart-failure finding to what is physically happening.
questions.why: Left-sided failure sends fluid into the lungs; right-sided failure sends it into the systemic veins. Each finding is the same pressure problem showing up somewhere different.
pairs: Crackles at the lung bases
Fluid forced from pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli
Pitting edema in the ankles
Systemic venous pressure driving fluid into dependent tissue
Pink frothy sputum
Alveolar fluid mixed with air and a little blood
Jugular venous distention
Right atrial pressure backing up the neck veins
Orthopnea
Lying flat shifting even more fluid into the chest
Hepatomegaly
Congestion swelling the liver behind the right heart

questions.stem: Why is a blood pressure taken in both arms when dissection is suspected?
questions.why: A dissection can extend into a subclavian artery and reduce flow down that arm. A difference of more than about 20 mmHg between arms is a red flag — and its absence does not rule dissection out.

options.t: Averaging the two arms gives a more accurate figure
options.why: Averaging is not the purpose of the comparison.

options.t: Cuff readings are inherently unreliable in one arm
options.why: Neither arm is inherently unreliable in a healthy vessel.

options.t: A difference confirms an infarct on that side of the heart
options.why: Infarcts do not produce arm-to-arm pressure differences.

options.t: A dissection flap can block flow into one arm

questions.stem: A patient's chest pain resolved completely after nitroglycerin. What does that tell you about the cause?
questions.why: Nitroglycerin relaxes smooth muscle everywhere, so it can relieve esophageal spasm as readily as angina. Response to a drug is not a diagnostic test — the patient still gets transported and worked up.

options.t: It confirms the pain was cardiac ischemia
options.why: Esophageal spasm and other smooth muscle problems also respond to nitrates.

options.t: Very little — relief does not confirm a cardiac origin
It rules out an infarct, since the tissue is still viable
options.why: Pain relief does not mean the infarct stopped evolving.

options.t: It means the patient can safely refuse transport
options.why: Resolved pain in a suspected ACS still needs evaluation.

questions.stem: MONA names the four ACS interventions. In what order does this program actually give them?
questions.why: The mnemonic spells MONA but the sequence is oxygen, aspirin, nitroglycerin, then morphine. Aspirin is the one drug with a mortality benefit, which is why it goes in early.

options.t: Aspirin, oxygen, morphine, nitroglycerin
options.why: Oxygen comes first and morphine last.

options.t: Morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin
options.why: That is the order of the letters in the mnemonic, not the order of treatment.

options.t: Nitroglycerin, oxygen, aspirin, morphine
options.why: Aspirin precedes nitroglycerin in the treatment sequence.

options.t: Oxygen, aspirin, nitroglycerin, morphine

questions.stem: Within what time of patient contact should the 12-lead be obtained, and what may be given before it?
questions.why: Ten minutes from patient contact. Aspirin and oxygen are the only things that go in first, because nitroglycerin and analgesia can alter the ST segments you are trying to capture.

options.t: On arrival at the hospital, where the equipment is better
options.why: The point of the field 12-lead is to activate the cath lab before arrival.

options.t: Within 30 minutes; any medication may precede it
options.why: Thirty minutes is well past the standard taught.

options.t: Within 10 minutes; only aspirin and oxygen precede it
Within 10 minutes; nitroglycerin may be given first
options.why: Nitroglycerin can change the tracing, so it waits for the 12-lead.

questions.stem: How is nitroglycerin dosed for cardiac chest pain in this program?
questions.why: 0.4 mg by tablet or spray, up to three doses at three to five minute intervals, with a blood pressure before each. Withhold it in a right ventricular infarct or after a PDE-5 inhibitor.

options.t: 0.4 mg sublingual tablet or spray, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes up to three doses
0.4 mg sublingual, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes with no dose limit
options.why: Three doses is the ceiling before moving to analgesia.

options.t: 0.4 mg sublingual as a single dose only
options.why: It is repeated if pain persists and the pressure allows.

options.t: 0.8 mg sublingual, repeated every 5 minutes up to two doses
options.why: The unit dose is 0.4 mg.

questions.stem: Into which three categories does the lecture sort a 12-lead in suspected ACS?
questions.why: Three buckets: STEMI, NSTEMI, or normal. The sort determines whether the cath lab gets activated from the field.

options.t: Ischemia, injury, and infarction
options.why: Those describe individual findings on the tracing, not the three-way sort.

options.t: STEMI, NSTEMI, and normal
Anterior, inferior, and lateral
options.why: Those are infarct locations, not categories of tracing.

options.t: STEMI, unstable angina, and stable angina
options.why: Angina is a clinical classification rather than a 12-lead category.

questions.stem: How does the lecture characterize heart failure, and what is its most common cause?
questions.why: It is a syndrome — a collection of findings produced by many different underlying problems — and coronary artery disease is the most common of those. Left-sided failure divides further into systolic and diastolic dysfunction.

options.t: A disease of the myocardium, most often caused by hypertension
options.why: The lecture is explicit that it is a syndrome, and names CAD as the leading cause.

options.t: A syndrome rather than a disease, most often caused by coronary artery disease
A disease of the conduction system, most often caused by dysrhythmia
options.why: Heart failure is a pump problem, not a conduction problem.

options.t: A syndrome rather than a disease, most often caused by valve disease
options.why: Valve disease is a cause but not the most common one.

questions.stem: What is cor pulmonale?
questions.why: Chronic lung disease raises pulmonary vascular resistance, the right ventricle works against it, and eventually fails. The presentation is right-sided: JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly.

options.t: Failure of both ventricles after a large infarct
options.why: Biventricular failure after infarction has a different mechanism.

options.t: Left heart failure caused by chronic hypertension
options.why: That is hypertensive heart disease, not cor pulmonale.

options.t: Right heart failure caused by left heart failure
options.why: That is the usual route to right failure, but it is not what this term names.

options.t: Right heart failure caused by lung disease

questions.stem: Which finding on a monitor accompanies pericardial tamponade?
questions.why: The heart swings inside a fluid-filled sac, so the QRS amplitude alternates beat to beat. Add Beck's triad — hypotension with a narrowed pulse pressure, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds — and the picture is complete.

options.t: Electrical alternans
A widened QRS with peaked T waves
options.why: That combination points to hyperkalemia.

options.t: Prominent U waves
options.why: Prominent U waves suggest hypokalemia.

options.t: Delta waves
options.why: Delta waves indicate an accessory pathway.

questions.stem: How does the lecture describe positioning and the fluid trial in cardiogenic shock?
questions.why: Sitting with the feet down reduces preload. A small 100 to 200 mL trial tests whether the patient is fluid responsive — withhold it if there are crackles or hepatomegaly, since those say the volume is already there. Then dopamine, norepinephrine, or epinephrine.

options.t: Supine with legs elevated; 1 liter saline bolus
options.why: Elevating the legs and a full liter both add preload the failing ventricle cannot handle.

options.t: Sitting up with feet dangling; 1 liter saline bolus
options.why: The position is right but the volume is far larger than the trial taught.

options.t: Left lateral recumbent; no fluid at all
options.why: A small trial is permitted, and that position is not what is taught here.

options.t: Sitting up with feet dangling; 100 to 200 mL saline trial

questions.stem: What diastolic pressure does the lecture use to define hypertension, and how often is pressure rechecked during treatment?
questions.why: Diastolic over 90 is the definition used. During treatment — labetalol in this program — the pressure comes every two to three minutes, because dropping it too far too fast is the danger.

options.t: Diastolic above 90; recheck once after the drug is complete
options.why: Titrating an antihypertensive requires repeated measurement, not one.

options.t: Diastolic above 100; recheck every 10 minutes
options.why: 100 is higher than the definition taught, and ten minutes is far too long.

options.t: Diastolic above 90; recheck every 2 to 3 minutes
Diastolic above 80; recheck every 5 minutes
options.why: 80 is below the number given, and the recheck interval is shorter.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of pericarditis, and what treats it?
questions.why: Most often viral, and NSAIDs are the treatment. The pain is positional — worse lying flat, better sitting forward — and the 12-lead shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

options.t: Autoimmune disease, treated with steroids
options.why: Autoimmune causes exist but are less common than viral.

options.t: Recent myocardial infarction, treated with aspirin alone
options.why: Post-infarction pericarditis is a recognized cause but not the leading one.

options.t: Bacterial infection, treated with antibiotics
options.why: Bacterial pericarditis occurs but is not the common cause.

options.t: Viral infection, treated with NSAIDs

questions.stem: How does an ascending aortic dissection differ from a descending one?
questions.why: Ascending dissections tend to occur in younger patients, are more severe, and can involve the vessels to the head and arms — hence the neurologic changes and a difference of more than 20 mmHg between arms. Descending dissections occur in older hypertensive patients and are generally less severe.

options.t: Younger patient, more severe, arm pressure difference over 20 mmHg, neuro changes
Younger patient, less severe, no neurologic findings
options.why: The ascending dissection is the more severe of the two and can produce neuro changes.

options.t: Older patient, more severe, with abdominal pain predominating
options.why: Abdominal pain suggests a descending dissection extending downward.

options.t: Older hypertensive patient, less severe, no arm difference
options.why: That describes the descending dissection.

questions.stem: What are the five Ps of acute arterial occlusion?
questions.why: Pain, pulselessness, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis. The distal limb is losing its blood supply, and the later Ps mark how long that has been going on.

options.t: Pain, pulselessness, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis
Pain, pulselessness, pallor, pressure, palpitations
options.why: Pressure and palpitations are not part of the list.

options.t: Pain, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
options.why: Poikilothermia appears in some versions but pulselessness is the one this lecture names.

options.t: Pain, pulselessness, pallor, perspiration, panic
options.why: Perspiration and panic are not part of the arterial assessment.

questions.stem: How does the onset of an arterial embolus differ from that of a thrombus?
questions.why: An embolus travels from somewhere else and lodges all at once, so the limb becomes symptomatic in an instant. A thrombus builds in place, so symptoms come on over time and collaterals have a chance to develop.

options.t: Both present gradually, over days to weeks
options.why: An embolus lodges abruptly and the symptoms start at that moment.

options.t: The embolus is sudden; the thrombus is gradual
The embolus is gradual; the thrombus is sudden
options.why: That reverses the two.

options.t: Both present suddenly, and history is the only difference
options.why: Onset is exactly what distinguishes them clinically.

questions.stem: Which three factors make up Virchow's triad, and what must you not do to a suspected DVT?
questions.why: Three factors: blood that is not moving, a damaged vessel wall, and blood that clots too readily. Homan sign — calf pain on dorsiflexion — supports the suspicion. Never rub or massage the leg; the clot's next stop is the lung.

options.t: Stasis, vessel wall injury, hypercoagulability — massage improves circulation
options.why: Massage risks dislodging the clot into the pulmonary circulation.

options.t: Stasis, infection, dehydration — never rub or massage the leg
options.why: Infection and dehydration are not the named factors.

options.t: Stasis, vessel wall injury, hypercoagulability — never rub or massage the leg
Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia — never rub or massage the leg
options.why: Those are coronary risk factors, not Virchow's triad.

questions.stem: Which angina is caused by coronary artery vasospasm and often shows ST elevation at rest?
questions.why: Prinzmetal is spasm rather than plaque, so it happens at rest and commonly elevates the ST segment. It carries a raised risk of dysrhythmias, acute MI, syncope and death despite the arteries being relatively clean.

options.t: Silent ischemia
options.why: Silent ischemia is defined by the absence of symptoms, not by vasospasm.

options.t: Stable angina
options.why: Stable angina is exertional and typically shows depression or T inversion.

options.t: Prinzmetal angina
Unstable angina
options.why: Unstable angina is plaque-driven and does not typically elevate ST segments.

questions.stem: What separates stable from unstable angina in terms of what the pain does?
questions.why: Stable angina resolves once the oxygen demand falls, showing ST depression or T inversion until it does. Unstable angina does not resolve, and the review sheet frames it plainly: a STEMI is coming.

options.t: Stable pain resolves with rest or nitro; unstable pain does not
Stable pain releases cardiac markers; unstable pain does not
options.why: Neither releases markers — that is what makes them angina rather than infarction.

options.t: Stable pain occurs at rest; unstable pain occurs on exertion
options.why: That reverses the two.

options.t: Stable pain radiates; unstable pain stays central
options.why: Radiation does not distinguish them.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a subendocardial from a transmural MI?
questions.why: Sub-endo-cardial: the inner layer under the endocardium, which is the region furthest from the blood supply and the first to die. Transmural crosses the whole wall and progresses faster. Infarcted tissue is always ringed by ischemic tissue that can still be saved.

options.t: Subendocardial is reversible; transmural is not
options.why: Both involve dead tissue; the difference is how much of the wall.

options.t: Subendocardial goes through the whole wall; transmural affects the inner layer
options.why: That reverses the two.

options.t: Subendocardial affects the inner layer; transmural goes through the whole wall
Subendocardial affects the right ventricle; transmural the left
options.why: Neither term refers to a specific ventricle.

questions.stem: Which artery is usually occluded in an inferior wall infarct?
questions.why: Inferior infarcts usually come from the RCA. Most infarcts overall involve the left ventricle and follow occlusion of the left coronary system — the inferior wall is the RCA exception you are expected to name.

options.t: The left main coronary artery
options.why: A left main occlusion produces a far more extensive infarct pattern.

options.t: The right coronary artery
The left anterior descending
options.why: The LAD supplies the anterior wall and septum.

options.t: The left circumflex
options.why: The circumflex supplies the lateral wall.

questions.stem: Why does the review sheet call hypotension with bradycardia the circle of death in ACS?
questions.why: A slow rate lowers cardiac output, which lowers coronary perfusion, which worsens the ischemia driving the slow rate. Put the patient at physical and emotional rest in semi-Fowler's, and take a blood pressure every five minutes.

options.t: Both are side effects of nitroglycerin
options.why: Nitroglycerin can drop pressure, but that is not what the phrase describes.

options.t: Low pressure and slow rate each worsen the other
Both indicate the infarct is complete
options.why: Neither finding tells you the infarct has finished evolving.

options.t: Both are contraindications to transport
options.why: Both make transport more urgent rather than less.

questions.stem: How should a limb with an acute arterial occlusion be managed?
questions.why: Gravity is the only help you can offer arterial flow, so keep the limb below the heart. Keep the patient warm generally, but do not apply heat or cold to the limb itself — the tissue cannot respond to either.

options.t: Keep it lower than the chest and warm, with no heat or cold applied
Elevate it and apply direct compression
options.why: Compression further reduces flow to a limb already starving.

options.t: Elevate it above the chest and apply cold packs
options.why: Elevation reduces what little arterial flow remains, and cold constricts further.

options.t: Keep it lower than the chest and apply heat
options.why: Applied heat raises the tissue's oxygen demand it cannot meet.
